Equivalence Relations

Group numbers by equal remainders. Then test three promises on everything to certify an equivalence relation.

An equivalence relation means 'on the same team'. Everyone is on their own team. Teaming is mutual, and it chains through teammates. When all three hold, the whole set splits into non-overlapping teams.

For example, split twelve 🧑 classmates into three teams of four. Nobody belongs to two teams at once. Inside a team, everyone matches everyone. Remainder classes look exactly like this.

Examples & Exercises

Prove completely that the relation a∼b  ⟺  n∣(a−b)a \sim b \iff n \mid (a - b)a∼b⟺n∣(a−b) on the integers Z\mathbb{Z}Z is an equivalence relation — pull each of the three conditions, reflexive, symmetric, transitive, down to the arithmetic of divisibility.

a∼b    ⟺    a≡b(modn)a \sim b \;\iff\; a \equiv b \pmod na∼b⟺a≡b(modn)
n∣(a−b),  n∣(b−c)  ⇒  n∣(a−c)=(a−b)+(b−c)n \mid (a-b),\; n \mid (b-c) \;\Rightarrow\; n \mid (a-c) = (a-b) + (b-c)n∣(a−b),n∣(b−c)⇒n∣(a−c)=(a−b)+(b−c)
Show proof

  1. Reflexive: for every integer aaa, a−a=0a - a = 0a−a=0 and n∣0n \mid 0n∣0, so a∼aa \sim aa∼a. In the scene at n=4n = 4n=4, all 121212 elements of UUU are related to themselves.

  2. Symmetric: suppose a∼ba \sim ba∼b. Then n∣(a−b)n \mid (a - b)n∣(a−b), so a−b=nka - b = nka−b=nk for some integer kkk, and therefore b−a=−nk=n(−k)b - a = -nk = n(-k)b−a=−nk=n(−k), giving n∣(b−a)n \mid (b - a)n∣(b−a), i.e. b∼ab \sim ab∼a.

    In the scene this is checked for all 122=14412^2 = 144122=144 ordered pairs of UUU.

  3. Transitive: suppose a∼ba \sim ba∼b and b∼cb \sim cb∼c. There are integers k,mk, mk,m with a−b=nka - b = nka−b=nk and b−c=nmb - c = nmb−c=nm; adding gives a−c=(a−b)+(b−c)=nk+nm=n(k+m)a - c = (a - b) + (b - c) = nk + nm = n(k + m)a−c=(a−b)+(b−c)=nk+nm=n(k+m), so n∣(a−c)n \mid (a - c)n∣(a−c), i.e. a∼ca \sim ca∼c.

    In the scene all 123=172812^3 = 1728123=1728 triples check out. The three conditions hold, so congruence is an equivalence relation.

Prove the partition theorem completely: for an equivalence relation ∼\sim∼ on a set SSS, (i) every xxx belongs to its own equivalence class [x][x][x], and (ii) if [x][x][x] and [y][y][y] share even one element then [x]=[y][x] = [y][x]=[y].

Deduce that distinct classes are disjoint and that the classes together cover SSS.

[x]={y∈S:y∼x}[x] = \{y \in S : y \sim x\}[x]={y∈S:y∼x}
z∈[x]∩[y]  ⇒  [x]=[y]z \in [x] \cap [y] \;\Rightarrow\; [x] = [y]z∈[x]∩[y]⇒[x]=[y]
Show proof

  1. (i) By reflexivity x∼xx \sim xx∼x, hence x∈[x]x \in [x]x∈[x]. So no class is empty, and every element lies in at least one class — the classes cover SSS.

  2. Setup for (ii): suppose some z∈[x]∩[y]z \in [x] \cap [y]z∈[x]∩[y] exists. By definition z∼xz \sim xz∼x and z∼yz \sim yz∼y.

    Symmetry turns z∼xz \sim xz∼x into x∼zx \sim zx∼z, and transitivity with z∼yz \sim yz∼y then gives x∼yx \sim yx∼y.

  3. Now show [x]⊆[y][x] \subseteq [y][x]⊆[y]. If w∈[x]w \in [x]w∈[x] then w∼xw \sim xw∼x; chaining w∼xw \sim xw∼x with x∼yx \sim yx∼y from the setup by transitivity gives w∼yw \sim yw∼y directly, i.e. w∈[y]w \in [y]w∈[y].

    Swapping the roles gives [y]⊆[x][y] \subseteq [x][y]⊆[x], hence [x]=[y][x] = [y][x]=[y].

  4. Conclusion: if two classes overlap at all, they are equal. Hence distinct classes are disjoint, and by (i) their union is SSS — an equivalence relation partitions its set into equivalence classes.

    In the scene at n=4n = 4n=4, the four classes split the 121212 elements of UUU into exactly 333 each.

Define a relation on R\mathbb{R}R by x∼y  ⟺  x−y∈Qx \sim y \iff x - y \in \mathbb{Q}x∼y⟺x−y∈Q. (a) Prove it is an equivalence relation, (b) determine the shape of its equivalence classes ([x]=x+Q[x] = x + \mathbb{Q}[x]=x+Q), and (c) explain why collecting one representative from each class of this partition is exactly the Vitali-set construction.

x∼y  ⟺  x−y∈Qx \sim y \iff x - y \in \mathbb{Q}x∼y⟺x−y∈Q
[x]=x+Q={x+q:q∈Q}[x] = x + \mathbb{Q} = \{x + q : q \in \mathbb{Q}\}[x]=x+Q={x+q:q∈Q}
Show proof

  1. (a) Reflexive: x−x=0∈Qx - x = 0 \in \mathbb{Q}x−x=0∈Q, so x∼xx \sim xx∼x. Symmetric: if x−y∈Qx - y \in \mathbb{Q}x−y∈Q then y−x=−(x−y)∈Qy - x = -(x - y) \in \mathbb{Q}y−x=−(x−y)∈Q, so y∼xy \sim xy∼x (rationals stay rational under negation).

    Transitive: if x−y∈Qx - y \in \mathbb{Q}x−y∈Q and y−z∈Qy - z \in \mathbb{Q}y−z∈Q then x−z=(x−y)+(y−z)∈Qx - z = (x - y) + (y - z) \in \mathbb{Q}x−z=(x−y)+(y−z)∈Q, so x∼zx \sim zx∼z (sums of rationals are rational). This is the same skeleton as the congruence proof in problem 1, with "divisibility" replaced by "membership in Q\mathbb{Q}Q".

  2. (b) [x]={y∈R:y−x∈Q}[x] = \{y \in \mathbb{R} : y - x \in \mathbb{Q}\}[x]={y∈R:y−x∈Q}; writing y=x+(y−x)y = x + (y - x)y=x+(y−x) shows this set is exactly x+Q={x+q:q∈Q}x + \mathbb{Q} = \{x + q : q \in \mathbb{Q}\}x+Q={x+q:q∈Q} — a shifted copy of the rationals, translated by xxx. Reals a rational distance apart are identified, and by the partition theorem (problem 2) these shifted copies tile R\mathbb{R}R without overlap.

  3. (c) Choosing exactly one representative from each class x+Qx + \mathbb{Q}x+Q and collecting them produces a Vitali set. But there are uncountably many classes and none has a "natural" representative, so this choice requires the axiom of choice — no rule can make the picks; the axiom only guarantees existence. In the integration chapter's vitali scene, this very set is shown not to be Lebesgue measurable.

    Take the representatives in [0,1][0,1][0,1] (every class x+Qx + \mathbb{Q}x+Q meets [0,1][0,1][0,1]), so V⊆[0,1]V \subseteq [0,1]V⊆[0,1]. The translates V+qV + qV+q for q∈Q∩[−1,1]q \in \mathbb{Q} \cap [-1,1]q∈Q∩[−1,1] are pairwise disjoint: if (V+q1)∩(V+q2)≠∅(V + q_1) \cap (V + q_2) \ne \emptyset(V+q1​)∩(V+q2​)=∅ then two representatives differ by q2−q1∈Qq_2 - q_1 \in \mathbb{Q}q2​−q1​∈Q, hence lie in the same class, hence are equal, so q1=q2q_1 = q_2q1​=q2​. They all have the same measure as VVV (translation invariance), they cover [0,1][0,1][0,1] (each x∈[0,1]x \in [0,1]x∈[0,1] differs from its representative by a rational qqq with ∣q∣≤1|q| \le 1∣q∣≤1), and their union lies in [−1,2][-1, 2][−1,2].

    If VVV were measurable with m(V)=0m(V) = 0m(V)=0, the countable union would have measure 000, contradicting that it covers [0,1][0,1][0,1]; if m(V)>0m(V) > 0m(V)>0, the union inside [−1,2][-1, 2][−1,2] would have infinite measure, again a contradiction. Hence VVV is not measurable.
